outcomes: Implement a forward diffusion schedule and explain signal, noise, and timestep coefficients with tensor shapes.
Train a timestep-conditioned denoiser with a noise-prediction objective and sample with gradients disabled.

sections.title: Turn clean data into a controlled noise experiment
sections.summary: Forward diffusion supplies training pairs by combining a clean sample with known Gaussian noise at a sampled timestep.
body: A beta schedule defines how much new noise enters at each step. From alpha_t = 1 - beta_t and the cumulative product alpha_bar_t, any noisy state x_t can be sampled directly from x_0 without simulating every earlier step. That direct formula makes randomized training batches practical.

Keep schedule tensors one-dimensional and gather the coefficient for each batch item. Reshape gathered values to [B, 1, ...] before multiplying an image or point cloud so broadcasting happens across feature dimensions rather than across examples.
points: x_0 and sampled noise epsilon have the same shape, dtype, and device.
Each example may use a different integer timestep.
alpha_bar near one preserves signal; alpha_bar near zero leaves mostly noise.
A fixed torch.Generator makes schedule visualizations reproducible.

code.title: Sample x_t directly
code.source:
import torch

def extract(values, timesteps, x):
    if values.ndim != 1:
        raise ValueError("schedule values must be one-dimensional")
    if timesteps.shape != (x.shape[0],):
        raise ValueError("expected one timestep per batch item")
    values = values.to(device=x.device, dtype=x.dtype)
    timesteps = timesteps.to(device=x.device, dtype=torch.long)
    gathered = values.index_select(0, timesteps)
    return gathered.reshape(x.shape[0], *([1] * (x.ndim - 1)))

def q_sample(x0, timesteps, alpha_bar, generator=None):
    if not x0.is_floating_point():
        raise TypeError("x0 must be floating point")
    noise = torch.randn(
        x0.shape, device=x0.device, dtype=x0.dtype, generator=generator,
    )
    keep = extract(alpha_bar.sqrt(), timesteps, x0)
    add = extract((1 - alpha_bar).sqrt(), timesteps, x0)
    return keep * x0 + add * noise, noise

x0 = torch.randn(4, 2)
alpha_bar = torch.linspace(0.999, 0.001, 100)
t = torch.tensor([0, 25, 50, 99])
xt, sampled_noise = q_sample(x0, t, alpha_bar)
assert xt.shape == sampled_noise.shape == x0.shape

callouts.body: Plot clean, early, middle, and late timesteps. A reversed cumulative product or a missing square root can still produce plausible-looking tensors while teaching the wrong process.

sections.title: Teach a model which noise was added
sections.summary: The denoiser receives x_t and t, then predicts the exact noise used to construct the training example.
body: A sinusoidal timestep embedding turns scalar time into features spanning several frequencies. A learned projection injects those features into each denoising block, allowing one network to solve many noise levels rather than training a separate model per step.

The common teaching objective is mean-squared error between predicted and sampled noise. Sample t uniformly, generate x_t and epsilon together, predict epsilon, and backpropagate the loss. Keep the target noise detached by construction; it is sampled data, not a parameterized result. Create one GradScaler before the training loop and reuse it; recreating it every step discards its dynamic scale history.

sections.title: Use a U-Net to mix local detail and global context
sections.summary: Downsampling expands receptive field, skip connections recover detail, and time features condition every scale.
body: A compact U-Net alternates convolutional blocks and spatial downsampling, then upsamples while concatenating encoder features. Every stage must document channel count and spatial resolution. Skip concatenation errors are usually padding or stride errors, so assert shapes before training for hours.

The diffusion schedule and loss do not depend on MNIST or CIFAR-10. The notebook progression deliberately moves from points to images: only x shape and denoiser architecture change. Normalize training images into the range expected by the final output and reverse that transformation only for display.
points: Time projections are reshaped to [B, C, 1, 1] before addition.
Skip tensors must match decoder spatial dimensions.
Display conversion is not part of the training graph.

code.title: Assert the denoiser contract
code.source:
import torch

@torch.inference_mode()
def assert_denoiser_contract(model, images, timesteps):
    """Check an injected denoiser on an already prepared batch."""
    if timesteps.shape != (images.shape[0],):
        raise ValueError("expected one timestep per image")
    model.eval()
    predicted = model(images, timesteps)
    assert predicted.shape == images.shape
    assert predicted.device == images.device
    return predicted

sections.title: Sample backward as a measured numerical procedure
sections.summary: Reverse diffusion repeatedly predicts noise and updates the current sample from the largest timestep to zero.
body: Initialize x_T from Gaussian noise, iterate timesteps in reverse, predict the noise component, compute the posterior mean, and add variance except at the final step. A sign, coefficient, or indexing error compounds across every iteration, so inspect intermediate states instead of looking only at the last image.

Sampling does not need gradients. Put the model in evaluation mode and wrap the loop with torch.inference_mode. Accept a generator and return tensors before visualization so correctness tests can compare repeated runs independently from plotting libraries. A supplied generator must target the same device as the random tensors it creates.

sections.title: Compile the hot loop and keep quality in the benchmark
sections.summary: Diffusion repeats the denoiser many times, making it a strong compilation target but also magnifying numerical mistakes.
body: Compile the denoiser rather than the Python sampling loop, data loader, or plotting code. Run an eager reference, compile, execute warm-up calls, synchronize the accelerator around timed regions, and test representative batch sizes and resolutions. Record cold compilation latency separately from steady-state latency.

A faster sampler is useful only if it preserves acceptable outputs. With a fixed initial noise tensor, compare eager and compiled intermediate predictions within tolerance. Then assess generated samples with the same qualitative grid or quantitative metric and report peak memory alongside latency.

code.title: Separate cold and warm execution
code.source:
from time import perf_counter
import torch

def synchronize_cuda(tensor):
    if tensor.is_cuda:
        torch.cuda.synchronize(tensor.device)

def compile_and_compare(model, xt, timesteps):
    """Return a compiled model plus separate cold and warm latency."""
    model.eval()
    compiled_model = torch.compile(model)
    with torch.inference_mode():
        eager_pred = model(xt, timesteps)

        synchronize_cuda(xt)
        start = perf_counter()
        _ = compiled_model(xt, timesteps)
        synchronize_cuda(xt)
        cold_seconds = perf_counter() - start

        start = perf_counter()
        compiled_pred = compiled_model(xt, timesteps)
        synchronize_cuda(xt)
        warm_seconds = perf_counter() - start

    torch.testing.assert_close(
        compiled_pred, eager_pred, rtol=2e-3, atol=2e-3,
    )
    return compiled_model, cold_seconds, warm_seconds
